title: Kearns v. Ford Motor Co. (2009)
summary: A consumer’s fraud-based challenge to Ford’s certified-preowned program lacked the required particulars of the representations and reliance.
notes:
The source distinguishes claims grounded in fraud from claims in which fraud is not an essential part of the theory. Rule 9(b) and general Rule 8 plausibility are related but separate questions.

Kearns sued under California's Consumers Legal Remedies Act and Unfair Competition Law; the Ninth Circuit (567 F.3d 1120) affirmed dismissal of his Third Amended Complaint, holding that claims 'grounded in fraud' under those statutes, including nondisclosure claims, must plead the 'who, what, when, where, and how' of the misconduct under Rule 9(b).

sections.Parties: Kearns, a purchaser of a certified-preowned vehicle, sued Ford and related defendants under California consumer-protection law.
sections.Material Facts: Kearns alleged that Ford promoted certified-preowned vehicles as receiving special inspections and assurances of quality, and that the program’s representations and omissions misled consumers. His amended complaint did not specify adequately the particular advertising or representations he encountered, when he encountered them, who made the relevant statements, or how the identified statements induced his purchase. Describing the overall program did not supply those missing particulars.
sections.Procedural History: After opportunities to amend, the district court dismissed the pleading. The Ninth Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Did the fraud-based consumer claims satisfy Rule 9(b), and could they avoid that rule by emphasizing nondisclosure?
sections.Holding: No. The claims as pleaded sounded in fraud and lacked the required particularity; the nondisclosure framing did not remove the defect.
sections.Reasoning: The court looked to the substance of the allegations rather than the statutory label alone. Because the theory charged a unified course of fraudulent conduct, Rule 9(b) required a sufficiently particular account to give defendants notice of the conduct to defend. Allegations about a program or general marketing campaign could not stand in for the plaintiff’s encounter with the challenged representations. The decision does not classify every consumer-protection claim as fraud; the pleaded theory matters.

learning.why: A consumer’s fraud-based challenge to Ford’s certified-preowned program lacked the required particulars of the representations and reliance.

topics.cp-fraud-pleading: Claims grounded in alleged fraud had to meet Rule 9(b)’s particularity requirement.
topics.cp-rule-scope: The federal pleading rule applied to the pleaded state-law consumer claims because of their fraud-based theory.
topics.cp-frcp-9: The case applies Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement to state consumer-protection claims that sound in fraud.
